requirement: Habeas MUST identify a Rust item by the pair of its `rust_file`, following the path rules in {cite}`requirements.ci.schema`, and a `rust_item` selector derived from a `syn` parse of that file. The selector MUST describe syntactic ancestry within the file and MUST NOT resolve Rust modules across files or use line numbers as identity. Named items MUST use kind-and-name segments such as `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments MUST distinguish inherent from trait impls using their syntactic self type and optional trait path. Otherwise identical selectors MUST have deterministic source-order disambiguators. A `use` declaration MUST have a positional selector `use#N`, where N is its one-based position among sibling `use` declarations; its import target MUST NOT form part of the selector. Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator. Selector spelling MUST be documented and reversible when names or types contain delimiter characters.
rationale:
**Verdict: the implementation looks complete, but the tests leave several MUST clauses unexercised, so I'm judging false.**

**What the implementation gets right (`src/rust_items.rs`)**
- `parse_items` parses with `syn::parse_file`. `ItemCollector` visits items, impl items, trait items and foreign items, and tracks a parent stack. Selectors are built from syntactic ancestry within the one file. There is no cross-file module resolution and no line-number identity.
- Named items use `kind[name]` segments through `named`, for example `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments are `impl[SelfTy]` for inherent impls and `impl[SelfTy/Trait]` for trait impls. They are built from the source text of the self type and trait path.
- Duplicates are grouped by `(parent, base)`, sorted by byte start, and given `#N` in source order. `use` and other unnamed items (`macro`, `item`, `Verbatim`) always get a `#N` ordinal, so `use` never includes its import target.
- `escape_segment` percent-encodes `% [ ] / #` and whitespace as UTF-8 bytes. Spelling is documented in `md/reference.md` (around line 370) and is reversible.
- The `{impl}` markers cover the relevant functions, and I found no unmarked selector-producing code. `parse_items` consumers in `add_input`, `inputs` and `authoring` only look selectors up.
- Minor smell: `add` takes unused `_name` and `_is_function` parameters. This is harmless.

**Test coverage**
- There is one unit test, `selectors_name_syntactic_ancestry_and_duplicates`. It checks:
  - `use#1` and `use#2`;
  - `mod[local]/fn[run]` and `mod[external]`;
  - inherent vs trait impl methods;
  - an escaped `impl[%5Bu8;%204%5D]` self type;
  - `trait[Trait]/fn[read]` and `extern[C]/fn[puts]`;
  - `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`;
  - `fn[repeated]#1` and `fn[repeated]#2`.
- The assertions only check that each expected selector is contained in the output. They do not check uniqueness or exact output.

**Gaps**
- The requirement says "Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator", but nothing tests the `macro#N` or `item#N` paths. Examples are macro invocations at item level, and impl, trait or foreign macro items.
- Reversibility is exercised only for one impl self type. Nothing tests escaping of names or the extern ABI, or the `r#ident` case. There is no round-trip or decode check.
- `use#N` is not tested as a position among sibling `use` declarations with other items interleaved, or inside a nested module. It also isn't tested that a changed import target leaves the selector unchanged.
- Duplicate disambiguation is tested only for plain `fn` siblings at the top level. It is not tested for duplicates under a parent, or for the same name under different parents.

I found no acknowledged FIXME for these gaps, so the determination is false rather than FIXME.

In `src/lib.rs`, `fn outer() { fn inner() {} }` gives the selectors `fn[outer]` and `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

In `src/lib.rs`, a method `run` in `impl Thing` has selector `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`; a method `run` in `impl Trait for Thing` has selector `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`; and a method `read` declared in `trait Read` has selector `trait[Read]/fn[read]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

A function `run` inside an inline `mod local { ... }` in `src/lib.rs` has selector `mod[local]/fn[run]`. A function defined in a separate `src/local.rs` file has a selector within that file, without reconstructing the path of a `mod local;` declaration elsewhere. A foreign function `puts` in an `extern "C"` block has selector `extern[C]/fn[puts]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

Two sibling declarations named `run` in one file, guarded by different `#[cfg]` attributes, have selectors `fn[run]#1` and `fn[run]#2` in source order. Their source line numbers are not part of either selector. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`

For consecutive sibling declarations `use alpha::A;` and `use beta::B;`, the selectors are `use#1` and `use#2`. Changing an import target leaves that declaration's positional selector the same and changes its raw evidence input. A named declaration such as `struct Packet;` instead has selector `struct[Packet]`. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors` {cite}`requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`

For a function preceded by a doc comment, an attribute, and an attached citation comment, a Rust-item input starts at the earliest attached line and ends at the function's final line. Its `text` contains those complete raw source lines. Inserting lines before them changes the displayed range without changing the input. {cite}`requirements.ci.rust_item_inputs`

For `impl Thing { fn run() {} }` on one line, `habeas add-input --for-requirement requirements.foo --rust-item src/lib.rs:1` adds separate inputs for `impl[Thing]` and `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`. Both contain the complete raw line. {cite}`requirements.cli.add_input_rust_item`

Each reference must name an existing requirement or example and is a directed edge between its source and that definition. Choose the role by what the source does:

- `{impl}`: the source implements part of the definition. It makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, is not implementing it. A requirement that refines another requirement's obligation can `{impl}` it. A convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the code that carries it out as a whole.
- `{test}`: the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies, either a test through its scenario and assertions, or a named example through its concrete case.
- `{cite}`: the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition without implementing or testing it.

Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. `{impl}` and `{test}` point from the definition to the source, so the source becomes a mandatory input to the definition's assessment, and that definition's evidence must cover the reference line. `{cite}` points from the source to the definition: a citing requirement or example receives the cited declaration as context, and the citing site needs no evidence coverage. Marking only `{cite}` on code that implements part of a requirement leaves a gap in that requirement's review. In the book, references and definitions become linked badges.

For Rust, Habeas parses first-party source files and requires every explicit function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, to have a requirement or named example reference in an attached comment or its body. Each named example references a requirement. A reference on an enclosing `impl` or module, in a string literal, or only in an evidence input does not cover the function. A Rust source file that cannot be parsed is reported as an error. For a helper with no behavior-specific requirement, agree on an explicit internal-detail requirement scoped to one area, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function's behavior; it cannot justify otherwise unspecified user-visible behavior. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_function_coverage` {cite}`requirements.cli.internal_detail_guidance`
